title: Best Periods to Make Wealth in Your Life
summary: How earning power, time, and compounding interact across each decade of life, and why the decade you start investing in changes your outcome by age 60 far more than the amount you contribute.
text: The Core Idea 20s = maximum compounding runway Time is your greatest wealth multiplier. 30s = income acceleration + consistency Build momentum and stay consistent. 40s = peak earning power Maximize and scale your capacity. 50s = catch-up + consolidation Close gaps and strengthen your plan. 60+ = preservation + income design Protect wealth and design steady income. · The Wealth-Building Timeline 20s Build skills, keep costs low, start investing early. 30s Grow salary, automate investing, buy quality assets. 40s Maximize savings rate, avoid lifestyle bloat, scale net worth. 50s Catch-up contributions, debt cleanup, retirement stress testing. 60+ Withdrawal planning, taxes, healthcare, legacy. · The best decade to start is now; the best decade for maximum compounding was earlier. · The Compounding Advantage Start Investing at Age Years of Compounding Value Multiplier by Age 60* What It Means Invest at age 25 35 years ≈ 10.7x Your money has the most time to grow and compound. Invest at age 35 25 years ≈ 5.4x Strong growth potential with less time in the market. Invest at age 45 15 years ≈ 2.8x Meaningful growth, but time works against you. Invest at age 55 5 years ≈ 1.4x Limited time to compound; focus on contributions. · *Assumes 7% annual growth to age 60. Illustrative only, not guaranteed. · Best Money-Making Windows Learning decade (20s) Biggest upside from skill stacking and discipline. Scaling decade (30s) Ideal for salary growth and asset accumulation. Peak earnings decade (40s) Strongest engine for net-worth acceleration. Optimization decade (50s+) Strongest for tax planning, asset allocation, and retirement readiness. · Wealth is usually built by a combination of skill growth, savings rate, and time in quality assets. · Priorities by Stage Stage Priorities 20s Emergency fund, employer match, Roth IRA, career investment 30s Max retirement accounts, taxable investing, insurance review, family planning 40s Diversify concentration risk, college/home balance, estate basics, higher savings rate 50s Catch-up contributions, healthcare planning, debt reduction, retirement modeling 60+ Withdrawal sequence, Social Security timing, Medicare, legacy planning · Golden Rules Start earlier if possible. Increase savings when income rises. Let compounding do the heavy lifting. Protect health, relationships, and earning power.

Momentum Invest consistently, accelerate growth, and expand assets. Financially secure Optimize taxes, protect wealth, and design for freedom. Work-optional & legacy Your money works for you—and for the people you love. · You don't need a perfect plan—just a plan you improve every year. Ranks 51–100 $30k–$75k $18k–$45k $65k–$80k Wide dispersion; great value schools can beat pricier schools above them Usually choose best fit + lowest cost + strongest major outcomes. · Illustrative 2025 estimates based on published cost of attendance ranges, salary reports, and college ROI research. Results vary by major, residency, and aid. · Is 20–100 Basically the Same? Partly True From about 20–100, the ranking premium flattens. A strong public flagship, honors college, or scholarship-heavy option can produce similar or better ROI than a more expensive private school. Not Totally True The best schools in the 20–40 band still tend to have stronger recruiting, alumni networks, and placement in finance, consulting, tech, law, and elite graduate programs. The Real Take Beyond the very top tier, rank matters less than debt load, major, internship access, graduation rate, and personal fit. · Where Rank Matters Most — And Least Career Path How Much Prestige Matters Investment banking / elite consulting Very high Quant / top tech / selective finance High Law / medicine prep Moderate to high Engineering / computer science Moderate — school matters, but strong publics can compete well Accounting / nursing / teaching Lower — licensure, skill, and debt usually matter more Entrepreneurship / general business Moderate — network matters, but execution matters more · Pay Whatever It Takes? text: The Big Idea A Historical Market Map A 19th-century cycle framework attributed to George Tritch and closely associated with Samuel Benner. Three Signal Types The model classifies markets into panic years, sell years, and buy years. B = Good Times to Sell The chart says prosperity and high prices are often the time to trim risk and take gains. C = Hard Times to Buy The framework treats low-price periods as opportunity zones for accumulation. Use as a Lens, Not a Law Interesting historically, but not a standalone investing system. · The Tritch Cycle Decoded A Periods Panic Years Meaning: panics, reversals, or bear-market stress Classical rhythm: 16/18/20-year sequence Investor posture: caution, defense, liquidity Modern translation: reduce fragility; avoid overconfidence B Periods Good Times / High Prices Meaning: prosperity, optimism, elevated pricing Classical rhythm: 8/9/10-year sequence Investor posture: rebalance, trim, harvest gains Modern translation: don't confuse euphoria with safety C Periods Hard Times / Low Prices Meaning: depressed prices and opportunity Classical rhythm: shorter recurring bottoming windows, often described as 3-6, 2-5, and 4-7-year sub-cycles Investor posture: accumulate quality assets carefully Modern translation: buy when fear is highest, if fundamentals hold · Traditional descriptions of the cycle are historical interpretations and should be treated as illustrative rather than precise market forecasts. · How Investors Try to Use It Identify the phase Ask whether the market feels panicky, euphoric, or washed out. Match the posture Defend in A, harvest in B, accumulate in C. Check the fundamentals Use valuations, earnings, rates, and breadth — not the cycle alone. Size risk carefully Never bet the portfolio on one timing model. Rebalance disciplined Use the cycle as a sentiment overlay, not a prophecy. · What the Framework Gets Right vs. What It Misses What the Framework Gets Right Markets Are Cyclical: booms, busts, and sentiment swings do repeat Extremes Matter: the best opportunities often appear when emotions are extreme Selling Is Part of Investing: taking gains and rebalancing is underrated Buying Fear Takes Courage: long-term wealth often comes from disciplined buying in weak periods What It Misses / Big Caveats No Guarantees: real markets rarely obey neat calendars Dates Drift: even if cycles rhyme, exact turning points are unreliable Macro Changes: rates, policy, technology, and geopolitics can overwhelm old patterns Valuation Still Matters: cheap and expensive are more useful than mystical timing Good Risk Management Wins: diversification and discipline matter more than prediction · Practical Money Map Takeaways Accumulation mode Use C-like weakness to buy quality assets steadily. Rebalance mode Use B-like strength to trim winners and restore allocation. Defense mode In A-like stress, protect liquidity and avoid forced selling. All-season mode For most investors, systematic investing beats trying to perfectly time every turn. · The value of Tritch's map is not perfect prediction — it is the reminder that markets move in cycles, sentiment swings, and disciplined investors prepare for both. · Educational infographic only. Historical framework, not financial, tax, or investment advice.

title: Optimized Selling Cycles & Timing for Stocks
summary: How to know when to trim, rebalance, harvest losses, or fully exit an equity position — replacing emotional selling with a staged, repeatable process.
text: Why Investors Sell Thesis changed The original investment rationale no longer holds true or has weakened materially. Valuation stretched Price has run far ahead of intrinsic value or peers and expected returns are now lower. Position oversized Position size exceeds target allocation or creates concentration risk in the portfolio. Better opportunity exists A higher-quality or higher-return opportunity is available elsewhere. Cash or tax need Need liquidity for goals or obligations, or to manage taxes more efficiently. · The Selling Ladder Partial trim When position grows far above target allocation. Rebalance When portfolio drift becomes material. Hold more than 1 year When possible for better tax treatment. Exit fully When the thesis breaks or business quality deteriorates. Harvest tax losses When useful and compliant. · Great selling is usually staged, not emotional. · Sell Signal Decision Matrix Signal Action Why Blow-off top / euphoric spike Trim or scale out Reversals after euphoria are frequent and drawdowns can be sharp. Fair value exceeded by a wide margin Trim or reduce Lower future returns likely when price is far above fair value. Guidance cut / earnings miss Reduce or exit Signals weakening fundamentals or deteriorating outlook. Break below major trend support Reduce or exit Technical breakdowns often lead to further downside and momentum shifts. Opportunity cost too high Trim or rotate Capital can earn more elsewhere. Focus on best risk-adjusted ideas. Personal liquidity need Trim or exit Meet goals or obligations without disrupting long-term plan. · Tax-Aware Selling Short-term vs long-term gains Hold positions over 1 year when possible to qualify for lower long-term capital gains rates. Offset gains with losses Use losses to offset gains (dollar-for-dollar up to $3,000) and carry forward unused losses. Spread sales across tax years if needed Stagger realized gains to manage tax brackets and avoid bunching income. Avoid panic selling on headlines alone Short-term fear drives mistakes. Let facts, fundamentals, and your plan guide decisions. · The Smart Exit Playbook Predefine target size Know your ideal allocation and position size before you buy. Decide trim bands in advance Set % bands for trims (e.g., +20%, +40%) and stick to them. Review fundamentals quarterly Confirm the thesis is still intact; update estimates and fair value. Rebalance concentration risk annually Reduce overweights and maintain a resilient, diversified portfolio. Keep a written exit thesis Define invalidation points and triggers in writing before you act. · The goal is not perfection — it is disciplined, repeatable decision-making.

title: Top Key Financial Indicators to Track for a Stock
summary: A practical scorecard for reading a stock across five families — growth, profitability, financial strength, valuation, and market behavior.
text: The 5 Indicator Families Growth Measures how fast the business is expanding. Profitability Shows how efficiently the company earns profit. Financial Strength Assesses balance sheet health and risk resilience. Valuation Determines if the stock price is fairly valued vs. growth and quality. Market Behavior Evaluates price momentum and investor sentiment. · Core Stock Dashboard Metric Why it matters What strong looks like Revenue growth Top-line growth drives long-term value. Consistent growth above industry. EPS growth Reflects earnings power for shareholders. Sustained double-digit growth. Gross margin Shows pricing power and cost efficiency. Above industry average and stable. Operating margin Measures core profitability of operations. Strong and steadily improving. Free cash flow margin Indicates cash quality and flexibility. Positive and expanding. Return on invested capital (ROIC) Measures how well capital generates returns. Above cost of capital (> WACC). Net debt / EBITDA Assesses leverage and financial risk. Below 2.5x (lower is better). Current ratio Measures short-term liquidity. Above 1.5x. P/E ratio Shows what you pay for earnings today. In line or below fair value range. PEG ratio Relates valuation to earnings growth. Below 1.5 (lower is better). Relative strength Compares price performance vs. market. RS rating 60+ preferred. Volume trend Confirms conviction behind price moves. Rising on up moves, low on pullbacks. · Red Flags Falling margins Shrinking margins signal pressure on profitability. Rising leverage Higher debt increases financial risk and limits flexibility. Weak free cash flow Low or negative FCF limits reinvestment and shareholder returns. Persistent share dilution Dilution erodes ownership and future returns. Negative earnings revisions Consistently lower estimates foreshadow disappointment. · Valuation vs Quality Map High quality + reasonable price Ideal zone Best combination for long-term outperformance. High quality + expensive Watchlist / trim carefully Excellent business, but limited margin of safety. Weak quality + cheap Value trap risk Cheap for a reason — high risk of further deterioration. Weak quality + expensive Avoid zone Poor fundamentals with high price — unfavorable risk/reward. · The Quick-Check Process Start with revenue and EPS trend Look for consistent acceleration. Confirm margin and cash flow quality Strong margins and positive, growing FCF. Review debt and balance sheet health Low leverage, solid liquidity, manageable risk. Compare valuation to growth Ensure price matches the quality and growth outlook. Check price trend and market confirmation Look for relative strength and supportive volume. · A strong stock usually combines durable growth, healthy economics, and a sensible valuation.

Broad Diversification Works Own stocks, bonds, and other assets across many regions and sectors. 2. Low Fees Matter Enormously Higher fees create a drag that can cost a fortune over decades. 3. Avoid Performance Chasing Past winners often disappoint in the future. Chasing performance destroys value. 4. Long Horizons Favor Discipline Staying invested through ups and downs has been rewarded over the long run. 8.
